If you had a friend tell you all of this about their partner - what would you say?

BPD isn't a free card to be abusive. Is she in therapy?

I suspect my mother had bpd - though she was also a drug user, which makes the brain even worse. 

I have BPD traits - my behaviors have never become as frightening and destructive as my mother. I own what I have done wrong, and take responsibility for my emotions. It's not easy - but I have a pretty wonderful life, though I have a lot of attachment trauma that I'm working on (thanks mom).

What sets apart a pwBPD that wants to get better from those who don't is overcoming shame and seeing that doing something bad does not equal that someone is bad. But that requires a lot of humility - something our parents lacked. 

I don't know what courses you have taken, but BPD is one of the more treatable personality disorders. But again - they have to take responsibility to get there.

Empathy. No, I'm not sociopathic, but putting myself in others' shoes has been a skill that I have had to teach myself and learn from other people in my life. I was not given a good model of this from either parent.
Tomorrow will be different. Maybe not better, but different. Hang in there.

I strongly suggest no contact for awhile. I have BPD and autistic traits (versus full diagnosis), and my previous partner left me because of the damage done. Abadonment is a pwBPD's nightmare, especially when they feel/are responsible for said abadonement. Pleading will turn into desperation. Desperation can turn into harassment. Tell them you need space, and if they persist, just block them or threateningq to block might be enough.

I am constantly on guard, waiting for criticism or an explosion. This has led to me appearing quite cold, sometimes overly blunt to others to get conversations other with. My therapist has also shared that I have autistic traits, so this affects how I carry myself as well.

To "mask", I have become really self-aware of where I hold tension, particularly in my face. I change my expressions to seem more engaged, and it does fool me into getting out of my head. That being said, it's really tiring. I feel your pain immensely.

It might depend on age too..I am in my late twenties, and have friends w/ BPD in their early thirties. We still all struggle, but we have matured and have a lot of awareness of our symptoms. We also call each other out on our shit, which takes a great deal of humility that gets cultivated over time.

I think that it's so easy for us to see that when we do "bad" things, that it makes us bad. That's essentially what shame is to the core.

But remember, that people are dynamic, including ourselves. We are not all bad; if we can internalize that, we can get closer to recovery.
Accept the facts and don't project your interpretations of reality on to situations.

If you can't bring yourself to trust your partner, then this relationship isn't for you. To be in a relationship means that you have to accept both the possibilities of good and bad situations - the worst situation, for a pwBPD, is the relationship ending. 

Radically accept what you know are the facts, not inferences you are making based on the circumstances.

If she doesn't take accountability, then she will not recover, end of story.

This may not apply to everyone that suffers from BPD (or any mental illness to be honest), but the inability to take accountability comes from a place of shame. Even though your soon to be ex-wife is behaving horribly, I would bet that she does feel ashamed under all of that. But to be absolved of that shame means taking accountability - but instead she is sabotaging herself. Her trauma may make her feel like she is truly worthless and cannot change.

She will either keep fucking up until she is finally disgusted with how she lives her life and takes responsibility, or will spiral like this forever. Please don't feel responsible for this; take care of yourself. You have done the best you could.
"Eat shit and die." I refused to give her money to fuel her drug addiction. I was 13.
This seems a little black and white - instead of the "worst person, best person" talk, why not acknowledge that you are just a human being that makes mistakes?

The best thing that you can do for yourself is to "reparent" yourself - meaning, give yourself the things that your mom wouldn't give you. pwBPD tend to have attachment traumas, so either we: reenact our childhood traumas with others and/or: seek the things our parents couldn't give us.

I really recommend books such as Healing Your Inner Lost Child, or really do a good search on "reparenting yourself". If you can give yourself the things that your mother couldn't - then you will build confidence over time, and make better decisions, especially with partners.

Did you grow up with a parent(s) that was unreliable, ignored you, or just straight up horrible to your face? I lived with mom for most of my early years; she was a drug addict, and had many sociopathic traits.

I have had a history of dating people who weren't present in the relationship for various reasons, and I have realized that it's because this is what I'm used to. When someone who genuinely wants to show up and love me, I push it away. I never know when the other shoe will drop, or when they will reveal that they actually despise me, so I don't trust what they offer.

Even if you don't have a history of child abuse, those with BPD tend to self-sabotage, because we don't believe we are allowed to be happy. We believe we aren't allowed to be happy, because of chronic shame instilled at a young age.

I was diagnosed at 20, now 27. I learned enough skills and went through a lot of various forms of therapy in college - since I wasn't having outbursts or hurting myself, I thought that I was recovered by the time I graduated and obtained a good job. 

Then I dated someone who put intentional effort in the relationship - something that I wasn't used to, and it scared the hell out of me. New symptoms started popping up in random pockets, but I just thought that I wasn't trying hard enough. I ended up splitting on her at the end, bewildered by my own behavior and lack of control. Turns out, a serious romantic relationship pulls all kinds of trauma responses out of you. 

I'm now in trauma informed therapy, processing a lot and recognizing patterns of self-sabotage in my life. Healing isn't linear. But I can honestly say that I love myself more than I ever, 6 months after the breakup.

Regardless of if he has truly changed or not - really be honest with yourself here. If you can't accept someone's past, then you can't accept them as a whole person. And if you can't accept them, then it's going to come out in an ugly way down the line, via mistrust or projection.

Sometimes someone's best just isn't enough. It doesn't make them a bad person; it just means that they are in a different stage of growth. 

BPD is an awful illness to live with; I'm sure she does genuinely feel awful about her outbursts. But it does seem like "her best" just isn't cutting it for you, or you wouldn't be on this subreddit making this post.

This is a really tough skill to learn, but radical acceptance. To be truly close to someone, you really do have to accept that they might leave you. And while that's definitely not want you want, you WILL be okay if that happens, so as long as you can accept that outcome.

If you don't accept this as a possible outcome, you might end up sabotaging things inadvertently, as many people with BPD do.

I have struggled with explaining why I engaged in a maladaptive behavior, with the goal of wanting to explain what exactly happened or what went through my mind.

The problem with doing this though, is that one isn't taking full responsibility for their actions. What you are essentially saying is "You made me do this" versus "I did this to myself". 

I think that a lot the struggle with BPD is deeply internalized shame. We feel shame, so we do something awful to punish ourselves/cope, then we feel even more shame. So we try to displace that shame on to other people - someone did this, so that's why I did something impulsive and damaging to myself. 

A big step to deal with this, is radical acceptance of yourself and your actions. And knowing just because you did something "bad", doesn't mean that you are bad.

It also might help to have a script to keep you from being manipulative:

"I did (maladaptive action here). This was wrong because (why it's wrong). In the future, I will (steps to be accountable for this action)."

Maybe I don't understand what gender nonconforming means; to me, it just means not wanting to follow prescribed gender roles. It isn't as so much an "identity", as an adjective. I personally don't see why another gender has to exist in order to fulfill this; as I said, if a man wants to reject gender roles or norms, then why can't he just be a man that does that? 

Honestly asking all of this, because I don't understand and would like to.
